source.title: Medium-sized protein language models perform well at transfer learning on realistic datasets
source.authors: Luiz C. Vieira; Morgan L. Handojo; Claus O. Wilke

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. The text identifies the published article as Scientific Reports (2025), despite the supplied venue and year metadata.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests how downstream transfer-learning performance varies with protein language model size and reports that larger models do not consistently outperform medium-sized ones. It does not measure pretraining cross-entropy or fit power laws.
record.gate_note: The study reports downstream R² results for protein language models across model sizes, including feature extraction and fine-tuning. It does not measure held-out pretraining loss, training tokens, compute, or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation; claims about language-model scaling laws in the introduction and discussion are citations or context, not results from this study. Compression-method and layer-selection results are not rows because they do not test the claim versions assessed here.
record.test_reason: The study compares downstream transfer-learning R² across protein language models of 8M–15B parameters, under both feature extraction and LoRA fine-tuning. This bears on V6 (downstream performance vs scale) in a new setting, protein LMs. It does not measure pretraining loss, tokens, compute or fitted laws, so V1–V5 and V7 are not tested. Size comparisons partly span different model families with different training data and schedules.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct, but incomplete. The authors conclude that larger pLMs do not consistently outperform medium-sized ones, especially when data is limited. Medium models (ESM-2 650M, ESM C 600M) fall only slightly behind the largest ones, and ESM C 600M with mean embeddings is a practical choice. They also state that larger models overall tended to do better, and do better with larger datasets. They add that their size conclusions hold for fine-tuning too.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates protein-language-model embeddings and downstream regression performance across model sizes, plus a limited LoRA fine-tuning comparison. It does not use the original language-model held-out-loss measurement or fit scaling laws.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors report that outcomes vary with dataset size and type, protein length, model family, and whether transfer learning uses feature extraction or fine-tuning. The model-size performance also varies across DMS and PISCES tasks.

fits_no_version.finding: Smaller ESM C models (300M, 600M) outperformed the much larger ESM-2 15B on DMS transfer. The authors attribute this to an improved training schedule rather than parameter count.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Downstream transfer performance depends on the training recipe and data more than on parameter count across model families.

record.problems: The study measures downstream protein-task R² rather than pretraining loss, and evaluates ESM-2 and related protein models rather than general language models. Most model-size results are presented in figures without exact values in the text. Fine-tuning was restricted to 31 DMS datasets meeting sample-size and sequence-length criteria, each model was fine-tuned once per dataset, and the authors could not fine-tune ESM-2 15B.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant model-size results were omitted. Compression-method and layer-wise results were left out because they do not test the claim versions evaluated here.

untested.parts: The relation between downstream performance and pretraining loss, any fitted functional form (power law) of downstream R² vs size, and conventional language-model tasks.

missing.what: Overall trend statement that larger models tended to yield better transfer results across both dataset types
missing.locator: Results, 'Moderately sized models perform well in transfer learning', Fig. 3A–B

missing.what: Downsampling curves: performance falls with fewer samples for all models. Models other than the smallest ESM-2 and the AMPLIFY models perform comparably at ≳10^4 samples. ESM-2 15B pulls ahead as it uses more Lasso features at larger sample sizes.
missing.locator: Results, 'Sample size drives transfer learning performance', Fig. 4, Fig. S7

missing.what: Fine-tuning overall: some improvement with size, leveling off around 650M across 31 DMS datasets (5 ESM-2 sizes, 155 runs)

record.verdict_notes: Protein masked LMs, downstream R² only. No size-controlled training: ESM-2 sizes share a recipe, but the ESM C and AMPLIFY comparisons are cross-family. The authors note that ESM-2 was not trained with data scaled to model size, which may limit gains at large sizes. Most per-model values are figure-only. r01, r02, r04, r07–r09, r13, r14, r20 and r25–r27 remain cannot_determine. The compression-method and layer-wise results are correctly left out.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss or power-law relationship with parameters, tokens, or compute is measured.
No small-run loss-law fits or large-run loss predictions are evaluated.
No fixed-compute budget allocation or compute-optimal parameter/token split is studied.
The study does not vary depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count to measure their effect on pretraining loss.
The study evaluates protein models and transfer-learning regimes, but does not test whether the same power-law form holds for pretraining loss in another modality or training regime.

Tests downstream prediction performance against model size for protein transfer learning, not the relation between downstream performance and pretraining loss or results on conventional language-model tasks.
The study does not compare fitted exponents or fitting choices, or test whether pretraining-loss curves bend away from a power law.

relationships.condition: Above ~150M–650M parameters within a family, and with limited task data (<~10^4 samples)
relationships.reason: Gains from large models were small or flat: 6B ESM C gave only a minor gain over 600M (r12). PISCES performance was comparable for all models ≥150M (r15–r24). ESM-2 150M slightly beat 3B on DMS (r03, r05). Fine-tuned 3B did not beat 650M (r28, r29). Larger models gained more only with more data.
relationships.display_finding: ESM C 6B gained little over 600M, PISCES performance was comparable above 150M, ESM-2 150M slightly beat 3B on DMS, and fine-tuned 3B did not beat 650M; larger models benefited more when more task data were available.
